story.title: David Walliams Faces Multiple Allegations of Sexual Misconduct and Grooming
story.summary: David Walliams, a British comedian and children's author, has been accused of sexual misconduct, including allegations of grooming minors and sexual assault of a 15-year-old. These claims emerged from a joint investigation by ITV News and The Guardian, which detailed accusations from multiple women. Walliams has denied the allegations, stating he is not a sexual predator and acknowledging past thoughtless behavior in casual relationships.

explore_lenses.label: What did the High Court actually decide?
explore_lenses.title: The ruling allowed reporting, not a finding of guilt
explore_lenses.summary: The High Court rejected Walliams’s request to block publication because of the claimed mental-health risk, but it did not decide whether any allegation was true.

claims.text: Mr Justice Nicklin said the case was not a trial of the allegations’ truth; it addressed only whether publication should be restrained by injunction.
The court dismissed the claim, while expressly stating that dismissal was not a finding that the allegations were true or approval of any particular publication.

Walliams broadly denied the allegations; in his response to the reporting, he said he had sometimes behaved thoughtlessly in casual relationships but denied abusing celebrity power, breaking the law, or being a sexual predator.

explore_lenses.label: Why did the investigation clear the public-interest bar?
explore_lenses.title: The outlets cited alleged abuse of status and broad sourcing
explore_lenses.summary: ITN and Guardian News & Media argued that the reporting concerned a prominent figure’s alleged use of status to pursue substantially younger women, in personal and professional settings.

claims.text: The court recorded that the proposed reporting concerned alleged use of Walliams’s status to establish contact with considerably younger women and engage or seek to engage in inappropriate sexual activity; some alleged conduct could be criminal if proved.
The Guardian and ITV News said their joint investigation heard from 30 sources with first-hand accounts; ITV said the reporting took three years to investigate.

The judge characterized the investigation as involving matters of substantial public interest and found that a publication ban would seriously interfere with press freedom and prevent sources from sharing their experiences publicly.

explore_lenses.label: What happens next legally and professionally?
explore_lenses.title: Police reports and institutional responses are the key next steps
explore_lenses.summary: The immediate publication dispute has ended, but any criminal process depends on people reporting allegations to police and on subsequent assessment; professional organizations have already begun responding.

claims.text: Walliams did not pursue an appeal by the deadline, allowing the reporting restrictions tied to his identification in the injunction proceedings to fall away.

As of November 10, the Metropolitan Police said it had received no related reports of sexual assault or other offences; it said any reports would be assessed and that complainants would be supported by specialist officers.
The BBC said it was removing some programmes and reviewing material featuring or written by Walliams; Independent Talent Group said it would no longer represent him.
Forecast: A criminal investigation would require reports and police assessment; no charging decision or active investigation was publicly confirmed as of November 10.

story_report.summary: British comedian and children’s author David Walliams has been accused of sexual misconduct, including grooming minors and the alleged sexual assault of a 15-year-old, in a joint ITV News and Guardian investigation. Walliams has denied the allegations, saying he is not a sexual predator. After he did not appeal a failed attempt to restrain publication, restrictions on identifying him in the injunction proceedings fell away, allowing the reporting to be published.

sections.heading: Court ruling did not determine allegations
sections.body: Mr Justice Nicklin said the injunction case was not a trial of whether the allegations were true, but concerned only whether publication should be restrained. The court dismissed the claim, while expressly stating that this was neither a finding that the allegations were true nor approval of any particular publication. Walliams broadly denied the accounts, acknowledging that he had sometimes behaved thoughtlessly in casual relationships but denying abuse of celebrity power, illegality or being a sexual predator.

sections.heading: Investigation examined alleged conduct
sections.body: The court recorded that the proposed reporting concerned allegations that Walliams used his status to contact considerably younger women and to engage, or seek to engage, in inappropriate sexual activity. It noted that some of the alleged conduct could be criminal if proved. The Guardian and ITV News said their investigation included 30 sources with first-hand accounts and took three years; the judge described the matters as substantially in the public interest and said a publication ban would seriously interfere with press freedom.

sections.heading: BBC and agent cut ties
sections.body: The BBC said it was removing some programmes and reviewing material featuring or written by Walliams. Independent Talent Group said it would no longer represent him. As of November 10, the Metropolitan Police said it had received no related reports of sexual assault or other offences, adding that any reports would be assessed and complainants supported by specialist officers.

unresolved.text: The injunction ruling did not resolve the underlying accounts or establish criminal liability, and the reporting process does not independently prove each individual allegation.
It is unknown whether any complainant will report allegations to police, whether police will open an investigation, or whether civil claims will follow.

related_stories.title: French Police Investigate Mohamed Al Fayed Properties for Trafficking and Abuse
related_stories.summary: French police have conducted searches at several properties, including the Ritz hotel in Paris, as part of an investigation into an alleged international network trafficking women linked to Mohamed Al Fayed. Arrests have been made, and the inquiry focuses on claims of sexual abuse associated with the late businessman's ventures. Other properties in Paris and Saint-Tropez were also searched.

related_stories.title: The law criminalized consensual sexual relations between male same-sex couples
related_stories.summary: A London court has overturned Trinidad and Tobago's law that criminalized consensual sexual relations between male same-sex couples. This decision marks a significant change in the legal landscape regarding LGBTQ+ rights in the country, which has been influenced by colonial-era laws.
